arml-1998-power-01a.prompt: *(Power Question 1998: Meditations on Partitions.)* Let positive integers $A$, $B$, $C$ be the angles (in degrees) of a triangle such that $A\le B\le C$. Determine all the values that each of $A$, $B$, and $C$ can take on.
arml-1998-power-01a.answer: $1\le A\le60$, $1\le B\le89$, $60\le C\le178$ (every integer in each range occurs)

arml-1998-power-01b.prompt: *(Power Question 1998: Meditations on Partitions.)* Let positive integers $A$, $B$, $C$ be the angles (in degrees) of a triangle such that $A\le B\le C$. Compute the number of ordered triples $(A,B,C)$ in which $B=70$.

arml-1998-power-02.prompt: *(Power Question 1998: Meditations on Partitions.)* In convex pentagon $ABCDE$, $m\angle A<m\angle B<m\angle C<m\angle D<m\angle E$. Let $T=m\angle C+m\angle D$. If $m\angle A:m\angle B:m\angle C:m\angle D:m\angle E=1:2:x:y:5$, determine the range of values of $T$.
arml-1998-power-02.answer: $252<T<300$ (open interval; $T$ takes every value strictly between)

arml-1998-power-07.prompt: *(Power Question 1998: Meditations on Partitions.)* Let $n>1$ be a positive integer. Allie and Bob play a game constructing a partition $n=a_1+a_2+\dots+a_k$ with $a_1\ge a_2\ge\dots\ge a_k\ge1$. Allie wins if there is an odd number of terms in the partition, i.e. if $k$ is odd; Bob wins otherwise. Allie begins by choosing a number $a_1$ between $1$ and $n-1$ inclusive. Bob then chooses a number $a_2$ between $a_1$ and $1$ inclusive such that $a_1+a_2\le n$. Allie then chooses an $a_3$ between $a_2$ and $1$ inclusive such that $a_1+a_2+a_3\le n$, and so on, with the game ending when the partition is complete. Determine with proof all $n>1$ for which Bob has a winning strategy.
arml-1998-power-07.answer: Bob wins exactly when $n$ is a power of $2$

arml-1998-power-08.prompt: *(Power Question 1998: Meditations on Partitions.)* Allie and Bob play a game similar to the one before ($n>1$, Allie first chooses $a_1$ between $1$ and $n-1$, and the player making the last move wins since Allie wins when $k$ is odd), except that the rule $a_i\ge a_{i+1}$ is replaced by $2a_i\ge a_{i+1}$ (each new term is at least $1$, at most twice the previous term, and the total never exceeds $n$). Prove that Bob has a winning strategy if and only if $n$ is a Fibonacci number. (You may assume that each positive integer $n$ can be uniquely represented as a sum of non-adjacent Fibonacci numbers, e.g. $32=21+8+3$.)
arml-1998-power-08.answer: Bob wins iff $n$ is a Fibonacci number (Zeckendorf / Fibonacci Nim argument)
